vignette:
Three months into our sessions, Captain Thomas Ryder still hesitates when describing that night. He sits forward in the chair, hands clasped, eyes fixed on a spot on the carpet. “I’d made that run a hundred times,” he says, his voice flat. “Coastal freighter, nine-man crew, containers of electronics and machinery. Standard transit out of the Gulf.”

The night of the collision, he remembers the radar showing a small vessel off the port bow—a fishing boat, he assumed, its lights dim or nonexistent. He had just stepped out of the wheelhouse for coffee when the first officer called. By the time he returned, it was too late. The freighter’s bow had sliced through the hull of a wooden charter boat carrying seventeen passengers. The impact didn’t feel catastrophic—more like a heavy thud, then a grinding shudder. But when he looked over the side, he saw pieces of debris and a slick of diesel spreading under the moon. Thirteen people died. Four were never recovered.

In the weeks after the Coast Guard inquiry, Thomas told his wife he was fine. He tried to go back to sea, but the moment he stepped onto the bridge his heart would hammer. He’d scan the horizon for anything that looked like a dark shape, any flicker of light that wasn’t official. His first officer noticed him checking the radar every thirty seconds, his hand trembling over the throttle. “You okay, Captain?” Thomas would wave him off, but his guts were twisting.

The nightmares started two weeks into the next voyage. He’d wake in his cabin, drenched and gasping, the sensation of the hull shuddering still vibrating through his bones. His wife, Susan, would lie beside him in their bed at home, trying to soothe him, but he’d push her away. “I don’t want to talk about it,” he’d say. Now, he finds himself avoiding the coast road, taking the inland highway home. He stopped watching the news because any mention of maritime accidents makes his chest tighten.

His crew has noticed changes. He’s become rigid about safety drills—running them twice as often as required, inspecting every life raft himself. He snaps at the deckhands when they laugh too loudly. “This is serious,” he tells them, his jaw set. “You think it’s a joke until something goes wrong.” He can feel the distance growing. His wife says he’s not himself; she finds him standing at the window at 3 a.m., staring into the yard.

On shore leave, Thomas avoids the marina. He stopped going to the dockhouse for coffee with other captains. When an old friend invited him to a memorial service for the fishing boat’s victims, he made an excuse. “I can’t,” he told Susan. “I don’t need to see their families.” But he knows the truth: he can’t bear the guilt. In sessions, his voice drops to a whisper. “I should have been at the wheel. I should have seen her sooner.” The PCL-5 score of 56 reflects what I see: hypervigilance, avoidance, intrusive memories, and a pervasive sense of shame that colors every interaction. He still captains his ship, but he’s running on autopilot, haunted by a night he can’t unstrap from the helm.
